I do this not because I don't like the question - I think it's a brilliant one, in fact - but because I worship chaos:

Pydro:

Years and years ago, when you had to buy minutes for the internet, I needed a name for my AOL account. Being into fantasy and magic, I combined "pyro" and "hydro" to get "Pydro." As people got to know that email address, it just became eaiser to use that as my screen-name everywhere.

Matchstickman:

If you look to the left you will see my avatar, that is Kevin Matchstick. He is a comic book character from a series called Mage: The Hero [D-word]. The first was "Discovered", the second "Defined", the third is slated to be "Denied".

The first series came out in 1984 and the second came out in 1997. During that time the writer and penciler, Matt Wagner, continued to work in the comic book industry and kept trying to get the second series produced, obviously eventually he did.

 

My name, Matchstickman, is a reminder to me don't drop your dreams, that if you keep at it you can get what you want eventually.

phantaskippy:

Phantaskippy came from shortly after my old Russian Blue Tomcat died when I was 19.  I don't know how many people can say they had a pet that truly belonged to them, but Skippy was mine.  We got him when I was 7 and he was very little.  He grew up to be a big cat (19lbs and 3 feet long stretched out) and was a really cool cat.  He could open doors, he ruled the neighborhood, he was nice to his kittens, he was a great cat.

I had a kind of sucky childhood, and for a number of years that cat was the only friend I thought I had.  He died at 12 years old, I was home on break  from school and he had been acting pretty sick.  His last night alive I held him as I sat on our bathroom floor and his body failed.  The next day I buried him under our Peach tree.  He was all black with a small white spot on his chin.

I got back to school and someone hacked my E-mail address, my new one I made in honor of my dead cat.  PhantaSkippy, the name stuck and I've become known by it enough online that I stick with it.  I honestly learnd more about being a man, a good person and a father from that cat than I did from so many men who tried to take that role in my life.  To this day it is a great reminder that we can find what we need in the most unlikely of places.

I'm sorry if this is more info than you really wanted, I could honestly go on all day telling stories about that cat.

jagarciao:

It's simply J. A. Garcia O. 

It's just my first and middle name initials followed by last name and then second last name initial. It's my gmail address so it was the default name when I signed up to the forum and I didn't know you could change it. By the time I figured out the username could be changed, well I just couldn't be bothered anymore…

Envisioner:

I've gone by Envisioner more often than not for the past 10 years; to me, imagination is more than just a way to keep oneself amused, it is the way that we project a future for ourselves and discover all of the possibilities that might await us.  I am a Dreamer and a Visionary in so many ways…and sometimes I kinda think I come from the future too.

imprimis5:

I use this username in many places. No joke, it came to me in a dream, during my college days of often-altered states. "Imprimis" means "in the first place" or "at the front." The "5" comes from, well, probably some plant somewhere. It stuck, and it's a hassle to change it or think up anything else.

Ronway:

It's not too interesting of a story actually. There is a game for the Playstation (even has a remake on the PSP that I wasn't too found of) called Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together. There is a character in said game that is named Duke Judah Ronway. He isn't really even a character that I liked, infact he was a bit of a jerk. I did like the name Ronway for some reason, i'm not entirely sure why it ended up sticking with me, but I have been using it for about a decade now for just about everything I do. At first I typically used it has a surname, Dryu was the one I used most often (Dryu is a name of a dragon ally in Shining Force Neo, that I was totally stoked for until I actually played it…), but the one I am probably known most by is Ronnie. That is because I was a lot more active in Maple Story with that name, then any other thing a did with Dryu Ronway. Though sometime after my Maple Story days, I started dropping the given names and only Ronway remained. These days, If Ronway is already taken on something, I tend to name it RonwayX or WickedRonway instead. As of right now, the only account I use semi-regularly that doesn't use Ronway is my GameFaqs account, which is DryuR. Bet you can't guess what the R stands for!

 

Before any of those names, for games I would name my character Rat. Or as I got a bit older and would giggle at swear words, I would use Damnrat. Monster Tamer was something I would use on the internet. There were a few more names inbetween Monster Tamer and Ronway, but during that time it was what ever I could think of at the time.

McBehrer:

So, I was in Forensics in High School. In case you don't know, it's kind of a catch-all for a number of performance-based competitions, including poetry/prose reading, improv acting, etc; some solo, some duets. One of them had me and a friend performing an improv scene, where we were given a setting and a cast of characters, and 15 minutes or so to create a scene; then we acted it out. In the scene, we were a couple of people in a bar; being very drunk, when asked my name, I started rambling about how I names were stupid and you should be called by something that fits you. "So… call me… Mc… Bear! Because… Mc is a name!"

"Because you're Scottish!"

"… Yeah, that too. And… Bear, because I'm big. And hairy.

… like a bear."

And I thought it was kind of a cool name, so I changed the spelling to seem more name-like, and it's been my username for things ever since.

Donner:

Donner is short for Donald R (for Robert).  It's a family name.  In Kindergarten they aske if I preferred Donner or Donald.  I figured kids would only call me names one way with Donner, so I chose it (plus it's what my family has always called me).

Nielzabub:

My name is Niel. For a while my handle was NielnotNeil because that's how people commonly misspell my name. When playing Rock Band 3, Reckless suggested naming my character Nielzabub. I liked it and have kept with it ever since.

BlueHairedMeerkat:

A few years back, a friend and I started a (short-lived) webcomic. It was, essentially, versions of our group of friends playing role-playing games in an attic during the zombie apocalypse, and the character who was 'me' had blue hair. It was posted on deviantART, and I didn't have a deviantART account, so when I wanted to comment on it I had to create an account, and I picked the username Blue-Hair.

The Meerkat got added after the third or fourth website's 'an account already exists with this username' message. I don't know why I picked Meerkat in particuar, I just liked it. It's the name I use most of the time now, though I'm BlueHairedKat or BlueMeerkat in some places with steep character limits.

Rabit:

My first name is Russell. (That matters later.) Got the nickname Rabbit in high school. When I got to college, I was on crutches for most of my freshman year and I ate a lot of salads (still do), so when one of the guys found out I had the nickname Rabbit in high school, it became a natural fit. It became so common, when my mom called the dorm and asked for Russell, she'd get confusion, but when she asked for Rabbit, the guys would immediately know who she was talking about. 

In our second-year apartment, we would write notes to each other about phone calls or other messages, planning for things coming up, etc., as we often went for extended periods without seeing each other (due to schedules, etc.). (Keep in mind this was before we had email.) Two of my roommates would spell my name as "Russel". I would harass them about how "it's spelled with two ls", but they decided to just stop using my name and started using Rabbit.

So, naturally, I had to explain that it was spelled with one b. 

From that point on, it was my default name on anything online that needed one.

XXVZ:

I got my "name" from other online accounts.

I could think of anything so I used X twice (my favourite letter) Then V (my secon favourite letter) then Z 'cause it sounded cool.

Not really a complicated story.

EvanDan55:

My full name is Evan Daniels. I've never minded sharing that with the Internet. So I've always used it, or shortened it to "EDan"

And I like the number 5 so much, I used it twice.

arenson9:

arenson, sure, but why 9? Well, long ago when the Internet was young, I had to pick a username and it occured to me that it would be cool to be able to keep using the same username as time goes by, but I'd seen how on AOL people often had to pick things like Smith373 because 372 other people were named Smith. I figured there wouldn't likely be nine other people who ever wanted arenson as a username, so if I just started with arenson9 I could probably always use it. So far, so good.

Theta_Sigma:

Theta Sigma is the designation used by The Doctor while he was in the Time Lord Academy. It's not his real name.

I use it in a number of different places, but it's not my only username (not by a long shot). Interestingly, it gets shortened in different ways, depending on where I am using it. Sometimes it's 'Theta', other places it's 'Sigma' or T_S or other variants.

Reckless:

My name is Brandon.  A friend once off-handedly referred to me as Reckless Abrandon (as in "reckless abandon").  From there, a lot of my friends started calling me Reckless.  Thus, my forum name.

Christopher:

As for my username… my name is Christopher. I'm super creative, folks.

SuperRick:

Superman is my favorite superhero and Richard is my first name.  I like Superman because there's very little moral ambuguity to him, generally speaking things are either right or wrong to him - black or white.  He never lies, and he doesn't meddle around much in the gritty gray areas of Batman - though he respects Batman and works with him often.  He's a protector, an inspiration, and a moral compass.

broccoli:

 As for my forum name, it came from an OLD show on MTV called Cartoon Sushi, where aspring cartoonists would send in their work to have it aired.  Specifically, this one  http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DT1YLp1NL_k

Braithwhite:

Basil Braithwhite was a mage I played for several campaigns with my homebrew roleplaying group.  He was proper, genteel, learned, and far too magically powerful for his own good.  He tended to talk first (for good or ill), talk second (usually for ill, at that point), and practiced ethical blood magic (in a world where those two things did not go together).

I picked it as my Enforcer handle, and its been my online name ever since.

Silverleaf:

Well, my forum name isn't that interesting a story really - it involves an old RPG character and an email address, but I'll give you a little more detail. 

It's 1997. I'm at school studying for A Levels, and I'm 17. My friend L starts dating D, who is possibly the geekiest person I've ever met. He's your stereotypical nerd - big glasses, gangly, poor social skills, mad hair, extremely intelligent, awkward, and besotted with L who doesn't yet realise that they are not at all suited to each other (incidentally, both are now happily married to other people). D attends a roleplaying club on Friday nights, and asks L to go with him. She asks me to go too, and because I'm a good friend I agree I'll go to keep her company. I plan to make some excuse to avoid it after that first time because it sounds a bit weird, to be honest.

And so begins my roleplaying career. At the club I meet some interesting people, and the gaming bug bites me pretty hard, beginning with a diceless Nightlife game and then moving into AD&D where the DM gives me a fighter who comes from a slightly magical pirate family who all share the same bright red hair and the surname Red. I give her the unimaginative first name Scarlett, and play her for years. I actually miss her, and should recreate her some time. 

I end up in a relationship with D's best friend C who also attends. We start going to LARP events, and I convert Scarlett to that system, and we decide, as LARPing couples often do (it's very embarrassing) to have an in-character wedding. The shame of it. Everything's arranged, but C manages to get his character killed just before the ceremony and I impress people with my acting skills, being able to actually cry over it (this is a skill I no longer have at all).

A little later I need a new email address, since my old Hotmail one is impossible to use anymore because no-one knew how to avoid getting spammed to death back then. I choose my new web mail provider, but scarlettred is unavailable. I can't think of anything more imaginative so I steal C's character's surname because I'm an idiot, and it just happens to be Silverleaf. And Scarlett Silverleaf sounds okay, I guess. 

I've used it on the internet ever since, but fairly quickly found that people called me Silverleaf or Silver rather than Scarlett. And now I'm used to it, and it's my primary 'net name and has been for a long time.

See, not very interesting.

As for my picture, the G+ crew were discussing their Paint villain avatars, and Envisioner suggested someone do the Ennead. So I did.

posts.cooked:
Right now, my favourite non-Sentinels game would probably be Penultima. It's just so much ridiculous fun.

The game is for 3-8 players, and in theory only needs a chess board, though I've seen it also use a Diplomacy board, SotM health tokens, dice, and pieces and decks of cards from several other games. The board is set up for a chess game, and two people (the players) are chosen to actually play the game, but the other people (the spectators) make up the rules for how the pieces move - and they don't tell the players. Instead, on their turn a player must ask yes/no questions about whether their pieces can move in certain ways. These questions can be as general ('can any of my pieces move to the far side of the board?') or specific ('can I move this rook onto his queen?'), and they can ask as many questions as they need, but if what they ask is possible then they're locked in to that course of action. Instead of moving a piece, a player can also (if possible) activate a piece for some manner of special ability, which are frequently ridiculous. The goal is to take the enemy king (unless somebody changes it, which is possible).

Highlights that I've seen include:

  • Dirty bombs that turn pieces they hit into mindless zombies.
  • A queen who shrinks the chessboard when activated.
  • Castles that, when moved, are deconstructed, carried across the board and eventually rebuilt on the target square.
  • Queens having affairs with enemy kings.
  • Pawns which, when captured, appear on a nearby Diplomacy board and must battle their way to the other side in order to return to the chessboard.
  • A king who earns money by being on the far side of the board, which he can then use to buy enemy pieces.

There are a lot of reasons it is my favorite game, but here are two:

1) No down time. You can lpay a game with eight people, and never feel bored.

2) Perhaps, more importantly, it has one of my favorite mechanics in any game: You can't get a new hand of cards, until you use all of your old ones. As is, it seems like all of the heroes work together well and, while they might have individual quirks and preferences (Ra calling Fanatic a lunatic, for instance), all of them get along and work together consistently as a cohesive, well-organized team.

I played Decipher's Star Trek CCG all through high school, since MtG was forbidden in my house. My senior year, I discovered the newly-released d20 Star Wars RPG. It was pulling teeth, getting players, but we managed it. In college, roleplaying really took off. Mostly RIFTS, but we tossed a few other things in there from time to time (d20 Modern and Exalted were the biggest repeat games), and Munchkin at the coffee shop (can you believe there were no expansions for it yet??). After college, I tried to keep roleplaying where I moved, but it was a rough time in my life and I didn't really have the wherewithal to find new players and run games. Cue a few years of gaming break. Then I moved again and began to find geeky friends. We played Magic every week, and it snowballed from there. The first "designer game" I bought for myself was SmallWorld, and I haven't stopped since, up to a collection of 250 games. Oh, and working for a tabletop gaming publisher.

Probably like most people I played mainstream boardgames (Monopoly, Scrabble, Cluedo, and card games like Rummy and Whist) as a kid with my family. Probably also like most people that tailed off and stopped as I got older (and my brother got older).

I always had a healthy interest in the fantasy genre and loved the TV show Knightmare, later discovered sci-fi and later still discovered pubs and boys and am dram.

But at 17 my friend Lauren started dating a guy called Dave who attended a games club on Friday nights and persuaded me to go along to keep her company. I planned to go once and then tell her it wasn't for me and never go again, but as it turned out she was the once who dropped it, not me. The people there were fun, my first RPG (a diceless version of Nightlife) was a good time, pubs happened after gaming, and I made a whole lot of new geeky friends. They introduced me to LARP, which I also loved.

I'm still attending, 18 years later. Lauren's married to a different Dave and hasn't played anything for years.

With knowing a lot of gamers, I naturally played some board games. I remember thing like Diplomacy, Axis and Allies, Battletech, Car Wars, Talisman, Munchkin, and some card game about a food fight. The games club has always owned a few board games bought with any subs money left over after paying for the venue, but somehow there came a point where I realised that I want to play LOTS more boardgames and started researching what would be a good fit for us.

(Of course, by virtue of living with the club organiser and being the club's board game expert and having room to store them, the hundred or so games we collectively own are rubbing shoulders with our smaller personal collection on my shelves. It's like having a games library that I didn't pay for, but can play whenever I want (or more accurately, whenever I can persuade people to play with me)).

And Sentinels happened.

When it comes to computer games I tend to like Fantasy-based RPGs (preferably first-person, because immersion), and also like some puzzle games (anyone else who likes them and hasn't yet played the Portal games, omg what are you waiting for?) and stuff.

Board game-wise I played mostly stuff like Monopoly, Cluedo, Scrabble, Careers, erm…what else did we play a lot…oh yeah, I also had (and still have, in my cupboard) the board games of the Crystal Maze (which I loved watching on telly), Knightmare (which I also loved watching on telly…and was a member of the fan club for a while, I recall), and a pirate-based one called Skull and Crossbones which came with a video but we only used that a couple of times and generally played without it.

When it comes to tabletop RPGs I'd heard of them for years…well, I'd mainly only heard of DnD, and played variants of it on the computer in the form of Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, and later Neverwinter Nights…but didn't get round to playing any till…hmm, I think it was probably late 2008 but I can't remember for sure. One of the forums I'm a member of (in fact, the one I've been a member of the longest, since March 2003) is dedicated to an RPG that came out in 1987 on the Atari and Amiga, called Dungeon Master. So it's the Dungeon Master forum. And a new member joined and made a post about how they'd had some experience at being a Dungeon Master and asking for advice on running games or something like that - they'd mistaken the DM in the forum's title for the other kind of DM, so some forum members posted to say hi and to point out the mistake but to say they were free to stick around and talk games with us anyway (this has happened a few more times in the past few years). That person never came back but the thread spawned a discussion amongst the rest of us about tabletop games and how I'd never played 'em 'cause I didn't know of anyone in my area who played. Ended up with someone linking a page they'd found which searches for gaming clubs in the UK, and from there I found one that was a couple of miles away and met two nights a week in the evenings, so I started going to that.

That was where I first played DnD, but was alos introduced to a bunch of other tabletop games, including all four Warhammer 40k RPGs (Dark Heresy, then Rogue Trader, then some time later Deathwatch came out, and finally Black Crusade), Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay (aka WFRP), Nobilis, World of Darkness,Traveller, Legend of the Five Rings, the Deadlands setting of Savage Worlds, and a bunch of others I've forgotten. Some people sometimes brought in card games and I can remember being introduced to Braggart, Ascension, and Chrononauts there, all three of which Ja'Ph' ended up getting for us to play (I'd told him about them as he wasn't there, in fact we may not have even been together quite yet) a few months or so later.

And Sentinels - someone at that club brought Sentinels, the original edition (pre-Enhanced), and Rook City, which was all that was available at that time. I found it fun, played the Wraith every time (because I thought her name was cool and I tend to like sneaky, Rogue-looking characters…so basically made my decision based on looking at her character card), and then the guy said that if anyone wanted to get it we should wait because they were gonna release an updated version in October, or something. So some months later (I think I'd stopped going to the club by this point) I remembered this and at some point I looked online (on a website called Games Lore, which sells RPG stuff) and found that not only was the Enhanced Edition of Sentinels out, but that there was another expansion in addition to the Rook City one I'd already seen, this one called Infernal Relics. Rook City was out of stock but I ordered the rest, getting Rook City when it came into stock about a month or so later. And we played Sentinels every weekend, multiple times, for well over a year. And at some point joined the forum, and hello :D.

I also rather like Traitor Mechanisms, but not in every game obviously, and only when they are really well designed ('Battlestar Galactica'- yes, 'Shadows over Camelot'- less so)

Least Favourite: Diplomatic Negotiations, Pacts, Treaties etc. - the short-lived kind which is always really far open to interpretation that you make in Diplomacy, Machiavelli or even Game of Thrones. You know, you and another player make a pact to attack a third player next turn, but when you move your troops in, you notice that your 'ally' is moving a sizable portion of his troops towards your now-weakened borders. I know, that's how you win the game and totally within the spirit of things, but I just can't bring myself to do stuff like that, especially not to my mates. I prefer the treaty mechanism that 'Twilight Imperium: Rex' uses (or Dune), where it is clear when you can make a treaty, when you can break it and what either party gets out of it. 

I majorly used to hate Auctions in games, by the way, but I got over that. Now I feel a bit meh about haggeling, but it's no dealbreaker for me.  

And I agree, Player Elimination is terrible.

Favorite:  Player Cooperation.  My three favorite games, all-time, are SotM, Arkham Horror, and Dead of Winter.  It might be the rpg-er in me, but I love working together towards a common goal, particularly when the game smacks you around, but you can still come around for a win.  Ghost Stories is another great one, as is Pittsburgh 68 (but I'm biased on the last one; I edited it).

2nd Favorite:  Unique player/character powers.  Again, it's the rpg-er in me, but I want my player to be different than yours.  Games that feature individual player powers really do it for me.

 

Least Favorite:  Lack of player interaction.  I hate games where what I do in the game has no bearing on anyone else, or our interactions are passive at best.  Most Eurogames have this as a hallmark, particularly worker placeent games, so I tend to avoid them like the plague.  Settlers of Catan, Lords of Waterdeep, Galaxy Trucker...yeah, keep those away from me.

2nd Least Favorite:  "Stock Markets" in games.  I find the stock market droll in real life; why would I want to play a simulation of it?

 

And, for the record, I actually don't mind player elimination.  Ca$h and Gun$ is a fantastic game that features player elimination, as is Cutthroat Caverns.  I much more deeply loathe the sorts of games where you're "effectively eliminated", such that you have 1-2 units left, but you can't actually leave, because it messes up the game dynamic for the remaining players.  Sitting there, unable to affect the board or play competitively, makes me angrier than being eliminated entirely.

Favorite:  Challenge.  I like a good challenge.  If I want to win easily I can play a video game and shoot 8 billion zombies with my fully-automatic rocket launcher with infinite ammo.  I play table games to be challenged.  Also this means a challenge that involves thinking and hopefully interaction with others, not just a high chance of losing.

Least favorite:  deck building games.  I haven't played one yet that connected theme to gameplay in any meaningful way.  They are disguised resource drafting games, I'd rather play Pit.

Bonus least favorite:  Victory points.  Largely intersects with the first.  We're fighting off the horde of monsters bent on destroying our land in hopes that we can score more points than the other fighters, and the monsters aren't even the source of the points?  WTF.  Games where points are a thematic conversion of success work alright, like ticket to ride, don't love the game, but the victory points work in that game, because your goal needs to be quantified.  Dominion is the worst game in the history of games.

Side note:  I have played Pittsburgh 68, because I'm from Pittsburgh and I love horror movies.  We were drunk, couldn't follow the rules and I'm not sure if we finished it or not.  It was at magfest, and drunken table gaming is most of my weekend there.

Bonus Side note:  Cash and Guns is the best drunken table gaming time I've had in a while, that is exactly how player elimination can work well.
